const path = "/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s087/discovery/prepared-20261005/87_13/luna/list.tsv";
const content = `strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.14.11\tendless smoke; no rest day or night\tThe commentary reads the continuing state in the fire as unrelieved, even without sleep or rest; Revelation says the beast-worshipers have no rest day or night and the smoke of their torment rises forever, giving a close image of conscious, unending punishment.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.20.10\ttorment day and night forever\tThe commentary stresses that the person remains in the fire without death or release; Revelation depicts the devil, beast, and false prophet tormented day and night forever, a direct parallel for punishment whose duration has no end.
strong\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:Rev.20.14\tlake of fire called second death\tThe commentary says the condemned person in the fire does not die; Revelation calls the lake of fire “the second death,” an explicit counter-description of the same final-fire image.
strong\tincil\tsoydas\tSBLGNT:John.11.26\tPeshitta cognates of Arabic ḥ-y-y and m-w-t\tThe commentary explicitly negates its Arabic verbs yahyā (“lives”) and yamūtu (“dies”); the Syriac Peshitta at this verse uses cognate life and death roots in Jesus’ promise that the one who lives and believes will never die, giving an opposite destiny in the same paired terms.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Deut.30.19\tHebrew ḥ-y-h and m-w-t; choosing life\tThe commentary’s Arabic yahyā and yamūtu mean “lives” and “dies”; Deuteronomy uses their Hebrew cognates for life and death when Moses sets the two before Israel and commands them to choose life, adding a covenantal choice to the commentary’s warning that preferring near life ends in neither life nor death.
strong\ttevrat\tkarsi_anlati\tMishnah Eduyot 2:10\ttwelve-month Gehinnom; consumed and scattered\tThe commentary presents the fire as a state in which death never comes; this Mishnah says the wicked are judged in Gehinnom for twelve months and then their bodies are consumed, their souls burned, and their ashes scattered, a finite and terminal account of punishment.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.14.10\tfire and sulfur; torment before the Lamb\tThe commentary identifies fīhā as the great fire in which the condemned remain; Revelation’s preceding verse depicts the beast-worshipers tormented with fire and sulfur, a specific shared image of final punishment.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.66.24\tcorpses; worm does not die; fire not quenched\tThe commentary says the person in the fire neither dies nor lives; Isaiah’s closing vision shows the corpses of rebels while their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched, sharing unending punishment imagery while locating endurance in the worm and fire rather than in living human victims.
medium\tincil\tyorum_gelenegi\tSBLGNT:Mark.9.48\tIsaiah’s undying worm applied to Gehenna\tThe commentary describes an ongoing state in the fire; Jesus invokes Isaiah’s undying worm and unquenched fire as Gehenna’s warning, carrying Isaiah’s judgment image into a teaching about a person’s final fate without saying that the person cannot die.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.16.24\tconscious anguish in flame; denied water\tThe commentary says the damned retain the capacity to feel pain and cannot find relief; in the parable the dead rich man is in anguish in flame and asks for water to cool his tongue, a concrete scene of postmortem sensation.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.16.26\tfixed gulf bars passage\tThe commentary repeatedly closes the possibility of leaving the place of punishment; Abraham says a great chasm prevents passage between the rich man’s place of torment and the place of comfort, a specific barrier though it separates abodes rather than describing an exit from Hades.
medium\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Luke.16.23\tthe dead rich man conscious in Hades\tThe commentary describes the condemned person’s continuing condition after entering the fire; Luke’s rich man is already dead yet conscious and tormented in Hades, offering a distinct Christian picture of postmortem awareness.
medium\ttevrat\tkarsi_anlati\tWLC:Dan.12.2\tsleepers awaken to two outcomes\tThe commentary insists that the person in the fire is neither dead nor alive; Daniel depicts sleepers in the dust awakening, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, a Jewish apocalyptic alternative in which the dead rise into one of two outcomes.
medium\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:John.5.29\tresurrection of life or judgment\tThe commentary’s double negation leaves no way out through either death or life; Jesus says the dead in the tombs will come out to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment, a contrasting Christian account of two postmortem destinies.
medium\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:Matt.25.46\teternal punishment opposite eternal life\tThe commentary places the damned in an unending state without life; Jesus’ judgment saying sends one group to eternal punishment and the righteous to eternal life, preserving the lasting divide while naming the condemned state as punishment rather than “neither life nor death.”
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Job.3.17\tthe dead rest; turmoil ceases\tThe commentary extends “does not die” to the denial of sleep and stillness; Job imagines Sheol as a place where the wicked cease turmoil and the weary rest, making the condemned person’s lack of deathly rest especially stark.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWisdom of Solomon 3:1\trighteous souls safe from torment\tThe commentary’s condemned person remains in torment without dying; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God’s hand and no torment touches them, a Jewish contrast between the punished and the protected dead.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWisdom of Solomon 3:4\thope of immortality\tThe commentary distinguishes mere endless existence from the full life of the hereafter; Wisdom says the righteous’ hope is full of immortality, a positive postmortem life sharply unlike the condemned person’s denied life.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\t2 Maccabees 7:9\tresurrection to eternal life after death\tThe commentary says the condemned person receives neither death nor life; the martyr says the King of the world will raise the faithful to renewed eternal life after death, presenting death as a passage to life rather than a closed state.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.21.4\tdeath ends amid comfort and life\tThe commentary notes that not dying can describe both the blessed and the damned, with the absence of life making the fire different; Revelation’s new creation has no more death, but its setting is God’s consoling presence, clarifying the difference between deathlessness with life and deathlessness without it.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.22.1\triver of the water of life\tThe commentary develops life as growth and ties living vegetation to life-giving rain; Revelation’s final vision has a river of the water of life flowing from God’s throne, a concrete image of the full life absent from the condemned person.
medium\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Luke.1.13\tZechariah’s promised son named John\tThe commentary links ayah 87:13’s verb yahyā (“lives”) to the prophet Yahya, whose birth was announced to elderly Zechariah; Luke’s angel answers Zechariah’s prayer and names the promised son John, paralleling the birth-announcement scene while the Greek name does not carry the Arabic life-wordplay.
medium\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Mark.6.16\tHerod says executed John has been raised\tThe commentary contrasts the condemned person who will not live with Yahya, whose death and being raised alive are blessed; after John’s execution Herod says he has been raised, a Christian tradition about the same prophet that turns on death and resurrection but appears only as Herod’s mistaken report.
medium\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Gen.3.22\tbarrier to eating the tree of life\tThe commentary recalls Adam’s descent from the garden and contrasts earthly life and death with the fire where neither occurs; Genesis says God bars access to the tree lest the human live forever, adding the Hebrew story’s distinct boundary around post-Eden life.
medium\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Gen.3.23\tAdam sent from Eden to work the soil\tThe commentary uses Adam’s descent to frame the earth as a place where people live and die; Genesis sends Adam from Eden to till the ground, supplying the corresponding expulsion scene and its mortal, soil-bound setting.
medium\ttevrat\tyorum_gelenegi\tBabylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17a\ttwelve months for some; others for generations\tThe commentary presents the fire’s state as unending; the Talmud assigns twelve months in Gehinnom and ashes afterward to some sinners but says other classes are confined for generations, showing how rabbinic interpretation differentiates the duration of punishment.
weak\ttevrat\tkarsi_anlati\tWLC:Eccl.9.5\tthe dead know nothing\tThe commentary’s fire preserves awareness and the ability to feel pain; Qohelet says the dead know nothing and their memory is forgotten, a contrary account of death, though its “under the sun” frame makes its relation to final judgment uncertain.
weak\ttevrat\tmotif\t1 Enoch 27:2–3\taccursed valley reserved for judgment\tThe commentary treats the fire as the lasting place of the condemned; Enoch describes an accursed valley where those cursed forever are gathered for judgment, a specific apocalyptic place-of-punishment image that does not itself say they neither die nor live.
`;
const quoted = content.replaceAll("'", "'\\''");
const res = await tools.exec_command({
  cmd: `cat > '${path}' <<'EOF'\n${content}EOF`,
  max_output_tokens: 2000
});
text(res.output || `Saved ${content.split("\n").length - 1} rows to ${path}.`);

medium\ttevrat\tyorum_gelenegi\tBabylonian Talmud, Berakhot 18a–b\trighteous called living after death; wicked dead while alive\tThe commentary distinguishes bodily death from moral and receptive “life”; a rabbinic maxim says the righteous are called living even after death and the wicked dead even in life, extending that secondary moral sense. medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.2.15\tlifelong slavery through fear of death\tThe commentary presents the condemned state as worse than an execution threat because death cannot release the person; Hebrews says fear of death enslaves people throughout life and describes Christ’s release from that bondage, a different Christian treatment of death’s power.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.38.18\tSheol and death cannot praise or hope\tThe commentary says the condemned neither dies nor lives after turning from reminder; Hezekiah’s prayer says Sheol cannot thank God and death cannot praise, distinguishing the dead from the living worshiper rather than describing an intermediate state.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.38.19\tthe living give thanks\tThe commentary links life with receiving reminder and the surah’s prayerful remembrance; Hezekiah says the living, the living give thanks to God, making the loss of life also a loss of ordinary praise.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Gen.3.19\tdust returns to dust\tThe commentary contrasts earthly existence, where people live and die, with the fire where neither happens; Genesis tells Adam he will return to the ground from which he was taken, specifying ordinary mortality in the Eden-to-earth frame.
